draft.title: A single superpower
card: A superpower is a state with global military, economic and political reach. During the Cold War there were two: the United States and the Soviet Union.
The Soviet Union broke up in December 1991. Russia was left much weaker, and no other state matched the United States in military and economic strength.
The United States was now the only superpower. This is often called a unipolar world, meaning one state held the most power.
In the 1990s many people hoped that the end of the Cold War would let states cooperate through the United Nations (UN). The two superpowers had often clashed there during the Cold War.
draft.remember: After 1991 one superpower was left, and many hoped the UN could now work better.

a.q: Why was the United States the only superpower after 1991?
opts: The Soviet Union broke up and no rival matched US strength
The Soviet Union merged with the United States in an alliance
The UN gave the United States control of its decisions
Russia grew stronger than the Soviet Union had been
a.why: The Soviet Union ended in 1991 and Russia was left weaker, so no rival matched US military and economic strength. The UN did not give the US control: the hope was for cooperation, not US rule.
a.clue: Think about what happened to the other Cold War superpower.

b.q: Which view best explains why some people in the early 1990s hoped the UN could work better than during the Cold War?
opts: The two superpowers no longer clashed there at every turn
The UN now had its own army that could not be challenged
The United States had left the UN to avoid involvement
Every state had agreed to give up its own armed forces
b.why: During the Cold War the superpowers often clashed at the UN. With that rivalry over, many hoped for more cooperation. This was a hope, not a certainty, and the card does not say the UN gained its own army.
b.clue: Recall who clashed at the UN before 1991.

proposal.title: A single superpower
card: A superpower is a state with global military, economic and political reach. During the Cold War there were two: the United States and the Soviet Union.
The Soviet Union broke up in December 1991. Russia was left much weaker, and no other state matched the United States in military and economic strength.
The United States was now the only superpower. This is called a unipolar world: one state held far more power than any other. The Cold War world, with two superpowers, was bipolar.

Many hoped states could now cooperate through the United Nations (UN), which Cold War rivalry had often split. In 1990 the UN Security Council backed force to push Iraq out of Kuwait, and US President George H. W. Bush spoke of a new world order.
proposal.remember: The Soviet collapse left a unipolar world and raised hopes that the UN could finally work as planned.

a.q: A historian describes the world in 1995 as unipolar. Which description fits that claim?
opts: One state held far more power than any other
Two rival superpowers balanced each other's power
Several great powers shared power fairly evenly
The UN held more power than any single state
a.why: Unipolar means one pole of power: after 1991 the United States had no equal. Two balanced superpowers describes the bipolar Cold War world, which ended when the Soviet Union broke up.
a.clue: Count the poles of power the word suggests.

b.q: In 1990 the UN Security Council backed force to push Iraq out of Kuwait. Why did this raise hopes for the UN?
opts: The Cold War rivalry that often split the UN had ended
The Soviet Union had broken up and no longer had a vote
The US no longer needed support from other states
It made the United States the world's only superpower
b.why: The UN had often been split by Cold War rivalry, so agreement on Kuwait suggested states could now cooperate. The Soviet Union did not break up until December 1991, after this vote, so it had not yet left the scene.
b.clue: Check the date the Soviet Union broke up.
